passages.title: Oath by the piercing star: every soul is watched
passages.tafsir:
# The Piercing Star and the Watcher Over Every Soul (86:1–4)

This short passage is a single sworn statement. In ayat 1–3 Allah swears a majestic oath — by the heaven and by the star that comes at night — and in ayah 4 He delivers the point the oath exists to drive home: *"There is no soul without a vigilant angel ˹recording everything˺."* The first three ayat build the setting; the fourth is the subject of the oath, the truth being certified. Everything else in the sūrah — the reflection on man's origin, the Day when secrets are laid bare — flows out of this opening declaration that every human being lives under watch.

## The Prophet ﷺ and this sūrah

Ibn Kathir opens his commentary under the heading "The Virtues of Sūrat at-Tāriq" with a narration recorded by An-Nasa'i from Jabir: Mu'adh once led the Maghrib prayer and recited al-Baqarah and an-Nisa'. The Prophet ﷺ said, "Are you putting the people to trial, O Mu'adh? Was it not sufficient for you to recite *As-Samā'i wat-Ṭāriq*, and *Ash-Shamsi wa Ḍuḥāhā*, and something like them?" In rebuking Mu'adh for burdening the congregation, the Prophet ﷺ pointed to this very sūrah as one that would have sufficed him — brief on the tongue, yet, as its opening ayat show, weighty in meaning.

## What is aṭ-Ṭāriq? The Qur'an asks, then answers

Ayah 1 swears "by the heaven and aṭ-Ṭāriq," and ayah 2 immediately turns to the listener: *"And what will make you realize what the nightly star is?"* This is the Qur'an's own way of signalling that something momentous is being named — it raises the question itself, then supplies the answer in ayah 3: *"the star of piercing brightness."*

**Ṭāriq — the night-comer.** The root sense of *ṭāriq* is one who arrives at night. Qatadah and others explained, as Ibn Kathir records, that "the star has been named Ṭāriq because it is only seen at night and it is hidden during the day." Ibn Kathir notes that this usage is supported by the authentic hadith that prohibits a man from coming to his family *ṭurūqan* — that is, arriving home unexpectedly at night. So the word itself paints the scene: the sky darkens, and the star arrives like a visitor in the night.

**Thāqib — the piercer.** The star is then described as *ath-thāqib*. Ibn 'Abbas explained it as "the illuminating," and 'Ikrimah added, "It is illuminating and it burns the Shayṭān." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān renders it "piercing brightness" — light so intense it seems to bore through the darkness. Which star is meant? Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that the word *najm* simply means "star," and the Qur'an does not specify any particular one, so it may be applied to any star; some commentators held that it refers to the Pleiades or to Saturn, citing examples of Arabic usage in support. The wording itself leaves it open — any brilliant star flaring in the night sky serves the oath.

Ibn Kathir sums up the scene under a striking heading: this is Allah "swearing by the existence of humanity surrounded by the organized system of Allah." The heaven above, the radiant stars set within it — an ordered creation, called as witness.

## Ayah 4: the subject of the oath — "there is a watcher over every soul"

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān pauses on the unusual grammar of ayah 4, and it is worth following. The particle *in* at the start of the ayah is here a *negative* particle ("no / not"), and *lammā* is an *exceptive* particle meaning "but / except" — a usage found in the dialect of the tribe of Banu Hudhail. So the ayah literally reads: "There is *not* a single soul *except* that over it there is a watcher (*ḥāfiẓ*)." The double negative makes the statement absolute: no exceptions, no one overlooked.

**Two meanings of ḥāfiẓ.** The commentators explain that the word *ḥāfiẓ* — literally "one who guards, keeps, preserves" — carries two complementary senses here, and both are affirmed:

1. **The recording angel.** *Ḥāfiẓ* can mean a guardian who watches over a person's actions and deeds so that the reckoning is made on that basis. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that although the word appears in the singular, it is used generically — there is not just one recording angel but a host of them, as another ayah testifies: *"While [appointed] over you there are watchers, who are noble, the writers [of the deeds]"* (82:10–11). An accurate, immediate record is being kept, and the reckoning will be made from it.

2. **The protecting angel.** *Ḥāfiẓ* can also mean one who protects from calamities. Ibn Kathir takes the ayah in this sense: every soul has a guardian over it from Allah that protects it from harm — as Allah says elsewhere, *"For him there are angels in succession, before him and behind him; they guard him by the command of Allah"* (13:11). These angels shield a person from every calamity except what Allah has decreed for him. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān also relays, from al-Qurṭubī, a tradition — cited without an isnad (chain of transmission) or any authenticity grading, so it should be received with that caution — reporting that Allah has appointed three hundred and sixty angels for every believer, protecting every limb, seven of them for the eye alone, driving away undecreed harm the way one fans away flies from a vessel of honey; were it not for these guards, the devils would snatch man away.

Hold the two meanings together and the ayah becomes both comforting and sobering: the same watchful care that shields you through every night you sleep is also faithfully writing down everything you do.

## Why the oath, and why this subject

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out the logic that binds ayat 1–4 to the rest of the sūrah. Allah swears by the sky and its stars to assert that a guardian angel is assigned to every human being, that a precise record of deeds is being kept, and that on the Day of Reckoning all secrets will be revealed. The rational conclusion, he writes, is that a person must ponder the consequences of what he is doing in this life — he should not, at any moment, lose sight of what is to happen on the Day of Reckoning. That is why ayah 5, immediately after this passage, calls man to look at his own humble origin; and the sūrah goes on to affirm (in verse 8) that the One who first created him is fully able to bring him back. The Watcher over you now is your Maker, and your Maker can raise you again.

There is also a quiet fittingness in the choice of oath. The *ṭāriq* is hidden by day and pierces the darkness by night — and the watcher over the soul is likewise unseen, yet nothing escapes him. Night, when a person imagines himself most unobserved, is precisely when the night-star blazes overhead.

## Living under the watch

The passage asks for one thing above all: awareness. Nothing you do — in public or in the dark, remembered or forgotten — goes unrecorded, and nothing about you goes unguarded. For the believer this cuts both ways. It steadies the heart: by Allah's command, angels before you and behind you guard you from every harm He has not decreed. And it awakens the conscience: the record is accurate and immediate, and — as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān summarizes the sūrah's message — on the Day of Reckoning all secrets will be revealed. To live these four ayat is to carry, at every moment, the calm and the carefulness of someone who knows he is never alone.

passages.title: Man's humble origin proves the resurrection
passages.tafsir:
This passage is a single, tightly built argument: Allah commands the human being to look honestly at the substance he began from, and then draws the conclusion — the One who produced him from that humble fluid is certainly able to bring him back, on a Day when nothing hidden will remain hidden and no one will be able to resist or rescue. Ayat 5–7 state the origin, ayah 8 states the conclusion, and ayat 9–10 state what that return will actually mean for us.

## "Let man look" (ayah 5)

The passage opens with a command: *fal-yanẓur al-insān mimma khuliq* — "So, let man see from what he is created!" Ibn Kathir explains the purpose of this command precisely: it is "alerting man to the weakness of his origin from which he was created," and its intent is "to guide man to accept (the reality of) the Hereafter." In other words, this is not biology for its own sake; the reflection is meant to lead somewhere.

The logic, as Ibn Kathir spells it out, is simple: "whoever is able to begin the creation, then he is also able to repeat it in the same way." He cites the parallel verse: "And He it is Who originates the creation, then He will repeat it; and this is easier for Him" (30:27) — and he notes that Allah has mentioned this proof in more than one place in the Qur'an.

## The gushing water (ayat 6–7)

Ayah 6 answers the question ayah 5 posed: the human being is created "from a water gushing forth" (*māʾin dāfiq*). Ibn Kathir explains this as the sexual fluid that comes out bursting forth from the man and the woman: "Thus, the child is produced from both of them by the permission of Allah." Note that last phrase: the fluid is the material, but the child comes into being *by Allah's permission* — the fluid itself creates nothing.

Ayah 7 then describes this fluid as "proceeding from between the *ṣulb* and the *tarāʾib*" — the backbone and the ribs. Here the commentators discuss what exactly is meant, and the sources record more than one understanding:

- **The classical majority view.** Ibn Kathir, representing the general body of commentators, takes the *ṣulb* (backbone, or loins) as referring to the man and the *tarāʾib* (the ribs, meaning the chest area) as referring to the woman. He cites a report through Shabib bin Bishr, from 'Ikrimah, from Ibn 'Abbas: "The backbone of the man and the ribs of the woman. It (the fluid) is yellow and fine in texture. The child will not be born except from both of them" — that is, from the contribution of both parents.

- **A reconciling reading.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, citing al-Baidawi, notes that embryological research describes the seminal fluid as gathering from the body through the spinal cord — the "representative of the brain" running through the backbone down to the loins, with branches reaching the chest-bones — so the classical explanation and the physiological picture need not be at odds.

- **Maʿārif's own observation on the wording.** The author of Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points out something easy to miss: the verse itself "does not specify man or woman." It simply says the water comes out from between the loins and the chest-bones. Since the chest is the principal organ of the front of the body and the loins of the back, mentioning the two together may be the Qur'an's way of saying *from the entire body* — of both men and women. On this reading the verse deliberately names the body's front and back landmarks to encompass the whole.

The differences here are differences of interpretation among the scholars, and the sources present them as such; what all readings share is the point the passage is driving at: your origin is a drop of fluid — humble, fragile, and wholly dependent on Allah's permission to become anything at all.

## The conclusion: "Verily, He is Able to bring him back!" (ayah 8)

Ayah 8 lands the argument: *innahu ʿalā rajʿihi la-qādir* — "Verily, He is Able to bring him back!" Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that *rajʿ* means "to bring back," and that the verse argues *a fortiori* — from the greater to the lesser: Allah, who created a full human being from a drop of seminal fluid, is all the more able to bring him back to life after death. Ibn Kathir makes the same point: He who could produce this man from gushing fluid "is able to repeat his creation and resurrect him to the final abode. This is clearly possible, because whoever is able to begin the creation then he surely is able to repeat it." And note what the resurrection is called here: *rajʿ*, a bringing *back* — a repeat of a creation already accomplished once.

## The Day the secrets are tested (ayah 9)

Ayah 8 said Allah *can* bring man back; ayah 9 says when, and what for: "The Day when all the secrets will be examined." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains the two key words: *tublā* literally means "to test, to examine," and *sarāʾir* means "secrets." So the Day of Reckoning is not merely a day when secrets leak out — they are *tested*, scrutinised, and laid bare. A person's beliefs, thoughts, motives and intentions that were hidden in this life, and the deeds done in secret that no one in this world ever knew about — all of it will be examined on the Plain of Gathering and made manifest. Ibn Kathir puts it the same way: "the secret will be made open and that which is concealed will be well known."

The sources give two vivid pictures of this exposure:

- Ibn Kathir cites the hadith confirmed in the Two Sahihs, on the authority of Ibn 'Umar, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Every betrayer will have a flag raised for him behind his back, and it will be said, 'This is the betrayal of so-and-so, the son of so-and-so.'" A wrong committed in concealment will be publicly named, with its owner identified.

- Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records, citing Qurtubi, the saying of 'Abdullah Ibn 'Umar that on the Day of Judgment Allah will disclose the secrets of all human beings: the sign of every good or bad belief and action will be displayed on a person's face, as beauty or as darkness and gloom, according to each individual's state.

## No power, no helper (ayah 10)

Ayah 10 closes the case: "Then he will have no power, nor any helper." Ibn Kathir parses the two negations exactly: no *power* — meaning nothing within himself; no *helper* — meaning no one from outside himself. On that Day, man "will not be able to save himself from the torment of Allah, and nor will anyone else be able to save him." Both escape routes — inner strength and outside rescue — are sealed. The being who began as a helpless drop ends the argument exactly as he began it: with no capacity of his own, wholly in the hand of his Creator.

## Living it

The passage itself tells the believer what to do with it, in its very first word: *look*. The command of ayah 5 is an act of worship available to everyone — honest reflection on one's own origin, undertaken (as Ibn Kathir says) to alert man to the weakness of his beginning and to guide him to accept the reality of the Hereafter. And ayah 9 gives that reflection its practical edge: if beliefs, motives, intentions, and the deeds no one sees will all be tested and laid bare on that Day, then the inner life is exactly where a person's real account is being written now — and it deserves the same honesty we are commanded to bring to our own origin.

passages.title: Oath by sky and earth: the Quran is decisive
passages.tafsir:
# The Oath of Sky and Earth: A Word That Decides

This short passage is a divine oath and its answer. Allah swears by two great, ever-repeating signs — the sky that keeps sending down rain (ayah 11) and the earth that keeps splitting open with new growth (ayah 12) — and then states what the oath is sworn for: this Qur'an is a decisive word (ayah 13), and nothing about it is jest or play (ayah 14). Two witnesses are called from creation, and then the verdict about revelation is given.

## The sky "of the return" (ayah 11)

The key word in ayah 11 is *ar-rajʿ*, from the root meaning "to return." Ibn ʿAbbās explained it simply as "rain," and in another narration from him, "the clouds that contain rain." He unpacked the word's force: "it rains and then it rains (again)." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives the same sense — *rajʿ* is the rain that comes down, stops, and then returns. The sky is not sworn by as a static ceiling but as a living cycle: water rises, falls, and comes back, season after season.

Qatādah drew out why this matters: the sky "returns the sustenance of the servants every year. Were it not for this, they would all be destroyed and so would their cattle." The oath, in other words, points at the very mechanism by which Allah keeps every creature alive.

## The earth "of the splitting" (ayah 12)

Paired with the returning sky is the splitting earth — *aṣ-ṣadʿ*, the crack. Ibn ʿAbbās explained it as the earth "splitting to bring forth plant growths," and Ibn Kathir records that this same explanation was given by a whole generation of early commentators: Saʿīd bin Jubayr, ʿIkrimah, Abū Mālik, Aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk, Al-Ḥasan, Qatādah, As-Suddī and others. Rain from above, growth from below — the two oaths belong together, for it is by the returning rain and the sprouting earth that, as Qatādah said, the sustenance of Allah's servants and their cattle is renewed year after year.

## "A decisive word" (ayah 13)

Now the answer of the oath: *innahu la-qawlun faṣl* — "surely this is a decisive word." The word *faṣl* carries the sense of separating and settling. Ibn ʿAbbās and Qatādah both explained it as "true," and another explanation recorded by Ibn Kathir is "a just ruling." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān brings the strands together: the Qur'an is a Decisive Word that decides between truth and falsehood, and there is no room for any doubt in it. It is not one voice among many in a debate; it is the verdict that ends the debate.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records here a saying of the Prophet ﷺ, narrated by ʿAlī (may Allah be pleased with him), describing the Qur'an: it is a book containing the accounts of the communities before you and the injunctions for those who come after you; "It is truly a Decisive Word. It is no joke." The Prophet's ﷺ own description echoes the exact wording of ayat 13 and 14 — *faṣl*, decisive, and not *hazl*, jest.

## "Not a thing for amusement" (ayah 14)

Ayah 14 states the same truth from the negative side: *wa mā huwa bil-hazl* — it is not *hazl*, amusement or joking. Ibn Kathir's comment is brief and complete: "rather it is serious and true." What ayah 13 affirms positively — a word that decides — ayah 14 protects from the opposite misreading: this word is nothing like jest.

## Why these two oaths for this claim?

The sources give the pairing its frame. Ibn Kathir's heading for this whole section is that Allah is here "swearing to the truthfulness of the Qur'an and the failure of those who oppose it." The sky that gives rain again and again, and the earth that splits open with growth, are summoned as witnesses; what they are summoned to attest is that this Book is true — decisive, just, and in earnest.

## Living it

The passage asks one thing of the reader: take this Book with the seriousness Allah Himself swears it deserves. If the Qur'an is *faṣl* — the criterion that separates truth from falsehood, "a just ruling" — then it is where a believer goes to have questions settled, not merely a text to admire. And if it is not *hazl*, then a casual, entertained relationship with it falls short of what it is. The One who keeps the rain returning and the earth splitting open has sworn by both that His word is final, true, and in deadly earnest.

passages.title: Their plotting, Allah's counter-plan, and brief respite
passages.tafsir:
# Their plotting, Allah's counter-plan, and brief respite (86:15–17)

These three short ayat close Sūrah aṭ-Ṭāriq with a quiet but devastating announcement: the enemies of the Qur'an are busy scheming against it, Allah declares that He too is planning, and the Prophet ﷺ is told simply to give them a little more time. What binds the passage together is a single contrast — human plotting set against divine planning — resolved not by argument but by patience, because the outcome is already decided.

The passage does not stand alone. Ibn Kathir reads ayat 11–17 as one connected movement, under the heading "Swearing to the Truthfulness of the Qur'an and the Failure of Those Who oppose it": Allah first swears that the Qur'an is "the Word that separates" and "not a thing for amusement" — in Ibn Kathir's words, "rather it is serious and true" — and only then, in ayah 15, turns to the people who scheme against so serious a Word.

## Ayat 15–16: plot against counter-plan

**"They are certainly devising plans" (ayah 15).** Ibn Kathir explains what this plotting was: the disbelievers "plot against the people in their calling them to oppose the Qur'an." Their scheming was not merely private disbelief; it was an active campaign to turn others away from the revelation — Ibn Kathir notes that they "reject Him and hinder others from His path."

**"But I too am planning" (ayah 16).** The Arabic sets the two side by side with the very same word: *innahum yakīdūna kaydan… wa akīdu kaydan* — "they are but plotting a plot… and I am planning a plan." Their scheme against the Qur'an is answered by Allah's own plan, and the sūrah leaves no doubt, in what follows, about which of the two will stand.

## Ayah 17: the command to wait

The conclusion is startling in its restraint. The Prophet ﷺ is not told to retaliate or even to answer the plotters. He is told, twice over: *fa-mahhil il-kāfirīn* — "give a respite to the disbelievers," which Ibn Kathir explains as "wait for them and do not be in haste concerning them" — and then *amhilhum ruwaydā*, "deal gently with them for a while." Ibn Kathir glosses *ruwaydā* as "a little while," and unpacks the threat folded inside the gentleness: "you will see what befalls them of torment, punishment and destruction."

The respite, in other words, is not a reprieve; it is bounded and brief. Ibn Kathir connects it to Allah's statement elsewhere: "We let them enjoy for a little while, then in the end We shall oblige them to (enter) a great torment" (31:24).

## Living it

The passage teaches the believer how to stand when opposition is organized and you are not. First, know that the scheming of the Qur'an's enemies does not go unanswered: against their plot stands Allah's plan. Second, take the command given to the Prophet ﷺ as your own discipline: wait, and do not be in haste. Patience here is not weakness or resignation — the enjoyment of those who war on the truth lasts only "a little while."

With these words the sūrah ends — and, as Ibn Kathir closes, unto Allah is all praise and thanks.
